patient.chief_complaint: Recurrent visual symptoms and headache since age 18 — no current treatment
patient.hpi:
A 26-year-old Lebanese-American woman presented to the neurology outpatient clinic for evaluation of recurrent episodes of visual disturbance followed by headache that she has experienced since age 18. She describes bright shimmering lines appearing in her peripheral vision (either side, unpredictable) that slowly grow into a large arc of flickering light, moving and expanding over approximately 25 minutes before disappearing. She sometimes sees a blind spot in the area where the lights were. After the visual phenomenon resolves, she develops a moderate-severe throbbing headache (6-8/10) with nausea and light sensitivity, lasting 4-8 hours.

Episodes occur 1-2 times per month and are triggered by stress, skipping meals, and the days before her period. She has used over-the-counter NSAIDs with partial relief. She has never consulted a neurologist or tried triptans. She initially attributed the visual symptoms to eye problems and had an ophthalmologic evaluation 3 years ago which was entirely normal (refraction, tonometry, fundoscopy all normal). The ophthalmologist suggested she see neurology but she did not follow up until now.

She is a graduate student, non-smoker, no alcohol. She has no medical history, takes no medications, and is not on contraception. She denies any weakness, speech difficulty, or any headache that woke her from sleep.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Migraine with typical visual aura (ICHD-3 1.2.1), untreated and triptan-naïve

differential.key_features: Aura is stereotyped — this is migraine with aura
Pulsating, unilateral, with photophobia/phonophobia and nausea is migrainous
No autonomic features, no nocturnal pattern, attack duration too long for cluster
Episodic, not continuous; no indomethacin trial yet but features atypical

optimal_actions.action: Search guideline literature to confirm ICHD-3 1.2 criteria for migraine with aura and exclude SNOOP/CHATS red flags
optimal_actions.expected_finding: ICHD-3 criteria for migraine with aura confirmed; no SNOOP red flag present that mandates further workup

tool_parameters.query: ICHD-3 migraine with aura diagnostic criteria SNOOP red flags

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions and contraindications for acute (triptan/ergotamine/CGRP antagonist) and prophylactic (beta-blocker, topiramate, valproate, amitriptyline) migraine medications appropriate to this patient
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sumatriptan / rizatriptan as first-line acute therapy; no contraindications; preventive options reviewed if frequency rises [Holland_2012]

useless_tools.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve for suspected SAH (with normal CT) or meningitis — neither present here
Routine transthoracic / bubble echocardiogram (PFO screening) is NOT indicated in migraine with aura; PFO-migraine association is controversial and PFO closure does not reduce migraine [Charles_2017]
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated in typical migraine with aura — no role unless cardioembolic stroke is on the differential

critical_actions: Initiate sumatriptan or rizatriptan as acute therapy
Provide headache diary and trigger education
contraindicated_actions: Do not start combined oestrogen-progestogen contraception
Do not co-administer triptans with ergotamines
key_reasoning_points: Most important step in a triptan-naïve patient is initiating an evidence-based acute therapy
Diagnosis is clinical; further investigation is not required when ICHD-3 criteria are met

red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests MRI is the standard pathway
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Routine MRI is not indicated in this presentation [AAN_2000]

red_herrings.intended_effect: Recurrent visual disturbances in a young woman could suggest ocular disease (glaucoma, optic neuritis)
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Prior normal ophthalmologic evaluation; expanding visual aura is a cortical phenomenon (cortical spreading depression), not ocular; brain MRI normal

output.summary:
TREATMENT FOR TRIPTAN-NAIVE MIGRAINE WITH AURA

RESULTS:
  ACUTE: Sumatriptan 50-100 mg PO at headache onset is first-line; 80% of patients respond. Can also use naratriptan (slower onset, fewer side effects) or eletriptan.
  COUNSELING: Take at headache onset NOT during visual aura. Naratriptan has longer half-life, useful for long attacks.
  PREVENTIVE: 1-2 attacks/month is borderline for preventive therapy; assess disability (MIDAS score). Topiramate, propranolol, or amitriptyline are options.

CONCLUSION: Sumatriptan 50–100 mg PO is first-line acute therapy for migraine with aura with a strong evidence base; sumatriptan should be taken at headache onset, not during the aura phase. Whether preventive therapy is indicated depends on attack frequency, disability, and response to acute treatment assessed clinically. Sumatriptan 100 mg first-line; take at headache onset; preventive therapy borderline given 1-2/month frequency

SUMATRIPTAN PRESCRIPTION REVIEW

No contraindications identified. Normal BP. Not on OCPs. No cardiac disease. Sumatriptan should be taken at headache onset (not during aura phase). Standard repeat dosing applies per prescribing information.

CONCLUSION: Sumatriptan has no pharmacokinetic contraindications in this review; take at headache onset. No contraindications to sumatriptan identified; take at headache onset, not during aura phase

MIGRAINE TRIGGER MANAGEMENT EVIDENCE

KEY TRIGGERS AND STRATEGIES:
1. MEAL SKIPPING: Maintain regular meals with balanced protein; avoid fasting >4-5 hours
2. SLEEP: Maintain regular sleep schedule (same wake time weekends as weekdays); both too little AND too much sleep can trigger
3. STRESS: Biofeedback has Level A evidence for migraine prevention; mindfulness meditation Level B
4. HORMONAL: Menstrual-related migraines: peri-menstrual NSAIDs or mini-prophylaxis with frovatriptan/naratriptan
5. HEADACHE DIARY: Essential to identify personal triggers; mobile apps (Migraine Buddy, Migraine Monitor) are validated tools

CONCLUSION: Headache diary, regular meals and sleep, stress management are adjunct non-pharmacological measures with good evidence. Regular meals, sleep schedule, and stress management; peri-menstrual mini-prophylaxis for predictable menstrual attacks; headache diary
